items.title: Cascadu interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, November 15, 2019
items.q: in Trinidad there was a drummer by the name of Andrew Beddoe. I mean when he played you were transported to another place altogether.

ctx.x: I think the drum has the ability to reach deeply into your soul. That’s the power of that vibrating membrane and that piece of wood. It has the power to call you. And there’s something spiritually that we respond to, that people respond to, just like you’re saying you know. You hear these drums and there’s something that you want to go and visit it. You want to be in the presence of that. And I think it’s a very primal call to the deepest part of our being. Because we’re all connected to that somehow or the other…

that place where we come from. Monk, I’ve seen, in Trinidad, there are people, and we have a very, very strong drum culture in Trinidad. And I have been to concerts in these big halls, You know people come in all — their suits, all suited up, and we come, we are a British colony for over 150 years, a Spanish colony for over 300 years etcetera. You know? And you know people will speak and dress in a very European way. And that drum would play in that concert hall. And people would start to, you know, dressed up in…

I didn’t even introduce you on film. This is Cascadú. And I can’t imagine that you ever play a gig where you are coasting. And by that I mean those of us who play gigs all the time, sometimes you’re playing and you know it’s just, you’re looking at your watch and oh man it’s only 8:15 and — when I was watching the three of you yesterday it’s hard for me to imagine that you would do that.
